nearest_whole_design.name: An assurance case (claim, argument, evidence) built under independent verification and validation, run on a supervision tree. The assurance case covers value faults: false, distorted or misapplied claims. The supervision tree covers crash faults: stall, crash, loop, reboot.
nearest_whole_design.source: Kelly, T.P. (1998), 'Arguing Safety: A Systematic Approach to Managing Safety Cases', PhD thesis, University of York (Goal Structuring Notation, GSN). IEEE Std 1012, 'Standard for System, Software, and Hardware Verification and Validation'. Armstrong, J. (2003), 'Making reliable distributed systems in the presence of software errors', PhD thesis, KTH (Erlang/OTP supervision trees).
nearest_whole_design.why_it_fits: The synthesis is the top claim and the field reviews are its sub-claims. Source cards are the evidence (GSN 'solutions'), a card's conditions are GSN 'context' and 'assumption' nodes, and 'not covered' is GSN's 'undeveloped goal'. External certification of an expert is the independent assessor, and the list of dismissals is the hazard log. At run time the tree is an OTP supervision tree. The coordinator supervises children and does no work itself, only reading status. Children supervise helpers. The single restart path is OTP's 'let it crash' with restart from a known state, and 'one repair' is a restart intensity of 1 followed by escalation to the parent.
nearest_whole_design.borrow_whole: From GSN: the element types (goal, strategy, solution, context, assumption, justification, undeveloped) and a mechanical trace from every claim to its evidence. A required counter-evidence (defeater) node on each top claim. From IEEE 1012: the three kinds of independence (technical, managerial, financial), and the rule that the V&V plan is fixed before the work starts. That plan includes every checker brief and every gate threshold. From OTP: the one_for_one restart strategy; a restart intensity (at most MaxR restarts within MaxT, then escalate to the parent); supervisors that hold only pointers and status; workers that hold the state.
nearest_whole_design.where_it_does_not_fit: (1) Assurance cases assume the evidence is stable and can be inspected, and that the assessors are humans who know different things. Here, evidence arrives through a fetch tool that loses content, and every assessor is the same model, so technical independence cannot be had and has to be measured instead (D4-01, D4-02). (2) Safety cases are known to turn into exercises in confirming what was hoped. Haddon-Cave, C. (2009), 'The Nimrod Review', HC 1025, The Stationery Office, describes this. It is the same risk as P2, so the defeater node is compulsory, not optional. (3) OTP assumes fail-stop errors that show up as a process exit. A language model's worst faults are value faults that never crash, so supervision cannot see them; the checks must. (4) An OTP restart costs almost nothing, but here one restart is a large share of the budget. MaxR therefore has to be about 1, not the usual 3 to 5. (5) None of this designs the shape (S) or the concurrency rules (P6, P7). That is the job of distributed systems and data structures.

mappings.classical_problem: Measuring how well a checker detects faults: its coverage, or diagnostic coverage. A detector whose rate was never measured reports 'nothing found', and that cannot be told apart from 'nothing there'. The tree has six checkers: the card checker, the citation check after the review, the quote script, the refuter, external certification, and the schema script. None of them has a measured detection rate.

solutions.name: Error seeding
solutions.source: Mills, H.D. (1972), 'On the Statistical Validation of Computer Programs', IBM Federal Systems Division report FSC-72-6015
solutions.guarantees: An unbiased estimate of the detector's detection rate, and of how many real faults remain.
solutions.assumptions: Seeded faults are found with the same probability as real faults. The detector does not know which faults were seeded.

solutions.name: Mutation analysis
solutions.source: DeMillo, R.A., Lipton, R.J., Sayward, F.G. (1978), 'Hints on Test Data Selection: Help for the Practicing Programmer', IEEE Computer 11(4)
solutions.guarantees: The mutation score measures whether a checker can tell small deliberate faults from correct items. Under the coupling effect, catching simple faults predicts catching complex ones.
solutions.assumptions: Competent-programmer hypothesis (real faults are close to correct items); the coupling effect holds.

solutions.name: Fault injection to validate error-detection mechanisms
solutions.source: Arlat, J., Aguera, M., Amat, L., Crouzet, Y., Fabre, J.-C., Laprie, J.-C., Martins, E., Powell, D. (1990), 'Fault Injection for Dependability Validation: A Methodology and Some Applications', IEEE Trans. Software Eng. 16(2)
solutions.guarantees: An estimate of coverage, P(detect | fault), with confidence bounds, for each fault class.
solutions.assumptions: The injected fault model is representative of real faults.

mappings.assumptions_that_fail_here: Representativeness. Nobody knows how a model's own fabrications are distributed. Mutants written by hand may be easier to catch than real errors, for example a number that is plainly out of place, or harder. If the same model generates the mutants, they share the checker's blind spots. A checker may recognise the style of the seeding. Outputs are not reproducible, so the detection rate is a distribution over runs, not one number. When representativeness fails, the field does three things. It builds mutation operators from the failure classes actually observed. It re-injects real defects found earlier ('defect reinjection'). It reports coverage per class, with confidence bounds, never as one pooled figure.

mechanism.rule: No checker is trusted until its detection rate has been measured for each fault class on blind seeded items. After that, every check batch carries a small seed as a proof test.
mechanism.runner: A Node script seed.js makes the mutants with deterministic operators applied to confirmed cards and to frozen copies of reviews. It writes the key to a folder that only the coordinator can read. A second script, score-seeds.js, scores the results. The coordinator starts both scripts. The checker sessions run with their fixed brief, which does not change and does not mention seeding.
mechanism.when: Calibration on the pilot field's outputs before wave 1. In every later wave, 5 to 10 % of each check batch is seeded items.
mechanism.input: Mutation operators: multiply or divide the number by 10; swap the number and its baseline; drop or alter one condition field (model, task, repository size); put the wrong card id in a citing sentence; take the quote from another card; a fabricated citation (real author names with a wrong year or title); widen a citing sentence beyond the card's conditions. Equal numbers of unmutated cards are added to measure false alarms.
mechanism.on_failure: If the lower 95 % bound of a class's detection rate is below the threshold the owner set in advance, the next wave does not start. The check is changed (its prompt, its batch size, or its model under F3) and measured again. Items that this checker 'confirmed' in that class are relabelled 'checked by an unqualified checker'.

mappings.formula_or_algorithm: Per fault class k: detection d_k = s_k / S_k, with a Clopper-Pearson interval (Clopper, C.J. & Pearson, E.S. (1934), Biometrika 26). Estimated real faults N_k = n_k * S_k / s_k, so the residual is N_k - n_k. Mutation score = killed / (mutants - equivalent mutants). Seeds needed to show d_k >= d0 at 95 % confidence with zero misses: S_k >= ln(0.05) / ln(d0). That is about 29 for d0 = 0.9 and 14 for d0 = 0.8. With zero misses in S items, the 95 % upper bound on the miss rate is about 3/S.
to_measure: S_k, s_k and n_k per fault class, per checker, and per batch size (detection may fall as the batch grows)
False alarm rate on unmutated, known-good items
Tokens per seeded item
Spread of d_k over two runs of the same checker
mappings.effect_on_measures: Hallucinations: the ledger's count of 'failed citations' becomes an estimate of the faults that remain. Quality: checkers that do not work are found before they are relied on. Tokens and cost: seeds add 5 to 10 % to check spend; calibration adds about 60 to 180 extra checks once. Time: small.
mappings.build_cost: Two Node scripts (about 250 lines) and a key folder. The calibration run is the main cost and depends on how many classes are seeded and on d0.

mappings.classical_problem: Common-mode (coincident) failure in design diversity, as in N-version programming and duplex comparison. Independently built versions fail together on the same inputs, so their agreement is weaker evidence than independence would predict.

solutions.name: N-version programming
solutions.source: Avizienis, A. (1985), 'The N-Version Approach to Fault-Tolerant Software', IEEE Trans. Software Eng. SE-11(12)
solutions.guarantees: Majority voting masks up to (N-1)/2 failed versions.
solutions.assumptions: The versions fail independently. N >= 3 for voting.

solutions.name: Coincident-failure model
solutions.source: Eckhardt, D.E. & Lee, L.D. (1985), 'A Theoretical Basis for the Analysis of Multiversion Software Subject to Coincident Errors', IEEE Trans. Software Eng. SE-11(12)
solutions.guarantees: Shows that even versions developed independently fail together more often than independence predicts whenever input difficulty varies: P(both fail) = E[theta^2] >= (E[theta])^2.
solutions.assumptions: The versions are drawn from the same population of developers and methods.

solutions.name: Experimental test of independence
solutions.source: Knight, J.C. & Leveson, N.G. (1986), 'An Experimental Evaluation of the Assumption of Independence in Multiversion Programming', IEEE Trans. Software Eng. SE-12(1)
solutions.guarantees: An empirical rejection of the independence assumption. Many coincident faults traced back to the shared specification.
solutions.assumptions: Student programmers and a single specification.

solutions.name: Forced diversity
solutions.source: Littlewood, B. & Miller, D.R. (1989), 'Conceptual Modeling of Coincident Failures in Multiversion Software', IEEE Trans. Software Eng. 15(12)
solutions.guarantees: Versions built by different methods can fail together less than independently, even below independence.
solutions.assumptions: The diversity is designed in along the dimension where the faults lie.

solutions.name: Consensus recovery block (comparison, then adjudication by an acceptance test)
solutions.source: Scott, R.K., Gault, J.W., McAllister, D.F. (1987), 'Fault-Tolerant Software Reliability Modeling', IEEE Trans. Software Eng. SE-13(5)
solutions.guarantees: Uses agreement when it exists, and falls back to an acceptance test when it does not.
solutions.assumptions: The acceptance test is independent of the versions.

mappings.assumptions_that_fail_here: Two instances of one model share one difficulty function theta(x), so the beta factor for their systematic errors is close to 1. Runs are not reproducible, so they show apparent diversity: a disagreement may be sampling noise and not a real detection, while agreement on a systematic error looks like confirmation. With N = 2 there is no majority, so a pair can detect a fault but cannot correct it. A second reviewer of the same frozen pack shares the pack as a common specification. That is the source of common faults that Knight and Leveson found, so it cannot see faults in the pack. When independence fails, the field: (a) uses comparison only to detect faults, never to vote; (b) sends every disagreement to an acceptance test, here the source-tied check; (c) forces diversity along the axis of the error, by a different model (F3), a different method (a perspective-based brief, or the contrary-evidence reader), or different inputs; (d) measures the coupling directly and does not assume it.

mechanism.rule: P3's rule ('agreement never raises a claim; a disagreement marks it weak, and adjudication is by checking the source') is standard: it is duplex comparison with adjudication by an acceptance test. What is missing is the rule for P20 and F2. A second opinion is admitted only along an axis where the measured beta is below a threshold the owner sets.
mechanism.runner: The seeding scripts of D4-01, run in the pilot on the same seeded set by every candidate second opinion: the same model reviewing the same pack; a different model, if F3 allows one; the same model with a different perspective brief. The coordinator reads the score file.
mechanism.when: In the pilot, before F2 is settled for later waves.
mechanism.input: The seeded review and card items of D4-01, with per-item miss indicators recorded for each opinion.
mechanism.on_failure: If beta is at or above the threshold (for example 0.7), that second opinion is not run in later waves, which also saves its spend. If no diverse option exists, the synthesis says 'no independent second opinion' rather than appearing to have one. Decide F2 by where the residual faults sit. If they are mostly faults in the pack (wrong selection of cards, missing contrary evidence), a second reviewer of the same pack cannot catch them; use the contrary reader or a second research run. If they are mostly reviewer faults (misused cards, wrong verdicts), use a second reviewer with a forced-diverse brief or model.

mappings.formula_or_algorithm: From the seeded items: p_A = miss rate of A, p_B = miss rate of B, p_AB = joint miss rate. Independence ratio r = p_AB / (p_A * p_B), where r = 1 means independent. Beta factor = p_AB / min(p_A, p_B), the beta-factor model of common-cause failure (Fleming, K.N. (1974), General Atomic report GA-A13284). Detection added by B = p_A - p_AB. Eckhardt-Lee: P(A and B both fail on input X) = (E theta)^2 + Var(theta).
to_measure: Per-item miss indicators for each opinion on one seeded set
Rate of disagreement on unseeded items, and the share of disagreements that adjudication resolves as noise
Tokens per second opinion
mappings.effect_on_measures: Tokens and cost fall when same-model second opinions that add no coverage are dropped. Quality and hallucinations improve, because a second opinion is used only where it measurably detects more. The synthesis reports its own independence honestly.
mappings.build_cost: Reuses D4-01, plus extra runs of each candidate second opinion during the pilot.

mappings.classical_problem: Where to put the correctness check in a chain of hand-overs: the end-to-end argument.

solutions.name: End-to-end argument
solutions.source: Saltzer, J.H., Reed, D.P., Clark, D.D. (1984), 'End-to-End Arguments in System Design', ACM Trans. Computer Systems 2(4)
solutions.guarantees: Correctness of the function as a whole can be ensured only by a check between the endpoints. Checks at each hop are only performance improvements: they make the end-to-end check fail less often.
solutions.assumptions: The endpoint has the means to check, which here is access to the original source.

mappings.assumptions_that_fail_here: The real endpoint is the owner, who cannot reopen every source. The source text reaches an agent through a small model's summary. Pages change, are rendered by script, are PDFs, or are behind a paywall. Only plain Node is available: zlib is built in, but PDF text extraction is crude. So the check moves to the last automated point that holds the original bytes. Those bytes are snapshotted and hashed when the card is taken in. What cannot be checked is labelled 'unverifiable', never passed (fail-safe default).

mechanism.rule: Every factual sentence in every review and in the synthesis is checked end to end by a script along the chain: sentence, card id, card fields, snapshot bytes. Typed hand-overs (P4) stay, as the per-hop performance measure. The P21 script must check the number and the condition fields as well as the quote. A quote match alone shows only that the passage exists.
mechanism.runner: snapshot.js, run by the child when a card is taken in (D4-04), fetches the page itself and stores its raw bytes, sha256 and fetch date in the field folder; the card records the hash. e2e-check.js is run by the coordinator after each review and again after the synthesis.
mechanism.when: Snapshot at intake. Check after each review, and after the synthesis, which is the owner's endpoint and is not checked today.
mechanism.input: Review and synthesis files whose claims are structured (card id, number, condition fields); cards.jsonl; the snapshots.
mechanism.on_failure: The result is three-valued: pass, fail, or not-run. A failed sentence is removed from the synthesis or marked 'unchecked'. A not-run sentence is labelled 'unverifiable' and counted, never passed. If a field's failure rate is above the threshold set in advance, its review goes back for repair.

mappings.formula_or_algorithm: The snapshot hash must equal the hash on the card. Normalise the snapshot text with NFKC, case folding, whitespace collapse and de-hyphenation, then search for the quote. Find the card's number in the text and report its distance from the quote. Then check: sentence.number == card.number and sentence.conditions == card.conditions, field by field, which should be exact because the fields were copied. Report the share of sentences that pass, fail and are unverifiable. Per hop, report which condition field was dropped and where.
to_measure: Share of sources whose text a script can fetch (HTML, PDF, blocked)
Rate of mismatch at each hop (reader to card, card to pack, pack to review, review to synthesis)
Rate of false mismatches caused by the normalisation
Share of claims labelled unverifiable
mappings.effect_on_measures: Hallucinations fall, and so does the loss at hand-overs. Tokens fall: a script does the quote and number part, and the model checker judges only whether a sentence stays within its conditions. Quality is now measured at the point the owner reads.
mappings.build_cost: Two Node scripts (about 300 lines) and disk space for the snapshots.

mappings.classical_problem: Containing defects within the phase that made them: inspect at each phase exit, because a defect found later costs more and has already been built on.

solutions.name: Design and code inspections with entry and exit criteria, recorded defects, rework and follow-up
solutions.source: Fagan, M.E. (1976), 'Design and Code Inspections to Reduce Errors in Program Development', IBM Systems Journal 15(3)
solutions.guarantees: Defects are removed before later work rests on them, and defect data is kept per phase.
solutions.assumptions: The inspectors are prepared and work at a controlled rate.

solutions.name: Cost of a defect rises with the phase that finds it
solutions.source: Boehm, B.W. (1981), 'Software Engineering Economics', Prentice-Hall
solutions.guarantees: An economic argument for inspecting early.
solutions.assumptions: Later work depends on earlier artifacts.

mappings.assumptions_that_fail_here: Amendment 3 moved the only card check to after the review, because 'no conclusion exists yet' earlier. But an unconfirmed false card sits in the expert's window while it reasons. It can shape judgment sentences that cite nothing, and the citation check never catches those. A defect found after the review means the review has to be redone. The field's answer is to put a cheap check at intake and keep the expensive judgment check where the conclusion exists.

mechanism.rule: Two checks. At card intake, the script part of D4-03 runs: quote and number found in the snapshot. A failed card is quarantined in quarantine.jsonl and never enters the pack. Exit criterion for gate A: every card in the pack passed the script or is labelled unverifiable. After the review, the model's judgment check runs on the cited cards (number, conditions, whether the citing sentence stays within them), as now.
mechanism.runner: intake.js, run by the child after each batch from a reader. The watcher counts cards that passed the script as progress (D4-06). The coordinator applies the exit criterion at gate A.
mechanism.when: At every intake (Stage A), and after the review.
mechanism.on_failure: The card is quarantined. If a reader's quarantine rate is above the threshold, that reader's whole batch is read again by a fresh reader.

mappings.formula_or_algorithm: Phase containment effectiveness = defects found at intake / (defects found at intake + defects of that kind found later, including seeded defects that escaped).
to_measure: Phase containment effectiveness for card defects
Tokens spent on rework per defect, by the phase that found it
Quarantine rate per reader
mappings.effect_on_measures: Hallucinations fall, because fewer wrong cards enter the expert's window. Token cost and time fall because there is less rework of reviews. The added cost is small, because the intake check is a script.
mappings.build_cost: Shared with D4-03, plus a quarantine file and a gate check.

mappings.classical_problem: Completeness of a hazard analysis: deriving a list of failure modes by a systematic method instead of judgment, and estimating what that list still misses.

solutions.name: STPA (System-Theoretic Process Analysis)
solutions.source: Leveson, N.G. (2011), 'Engineering a Safer World: Systems Thinking Applied to Safety', MIT Press
solutions.guarantees: Systematic coverage relative to a model of the control structure. Every control action is examined against four types of unsafe control action.
solutions.assumptions: The control-structure model is correct and complete.

solutions.name: FMEA
solutions.source: MIL-STD-1629A (1980), 'Procedures for Performing a Failure Mode, Effects and Criticality Analysis'
solutions.guarantees: Every component is crossed with every failure mode in a list of modes.
solutions.assumptions: The component list and the list of modes are complete. Single failures only.

solutions.name: Fault tree analysis
solutions.source: Vesely, W.E., Goldberg, F.F., Roberts, N.H., Haasl, D.F. (1981), 'Fault Tree Handbook', NUREG-0492, US Nuclear Regulatory Commission
solutions.guarantees: Minimal cut sets for a named top event (for example 'a false claim reaches the owner').
solutions.assumptions: The top event and its decomposition are right.

solutions.name: Taxonomy of failure modes (guide words)
solutions.source: Avizienis, A., Laprie, J.-C., Randell, B., Landwehr, C. (2004), 'Basic Concepts and Taxonomy of Dependable and Secure Computing', IEEE Trans. Dependable and Secure Computing 1(1)
solutions.guarantees: A standard set of failure modes: content or timing; halt or erratic; signalled or unsignalled; consistent or inconsistent across readers.
solutions.assumptions: None that matter here.

solutions.name: Capture-recapture estimate of defects missed by inspectors
solutions.source: Eick, S.G., Loader, C.R., Long, M.D., Votta, L.G., Vander Wiel, S. (1992), 'Estimating Software Fault Content Before Coding', Proc. ICSE 14
solutions.guarantees: An estimate of the total number of defects, and so of how many remain unfound.
solutions.assumptions: Inspectors find defects independently and with similar probabilities.

mappings.assumptions_that_fail_here: Two same-model analysts are not independent, so the capture-recapture estimate is biased low. The fix is diversity of method: STPA against FMEA, not two runs of one method. The control-structure model would be drawn by the coordinator, the party under analysis. Failure-mode libraries made for hardware lack the language-model modes: fabrication, following injected text, agreeing with the brief. These are added as guide words. No method proves completeness. The field claims a method, its model, an estimate of the residual, and feedback from operation.

mechanism.rule: The problem list is derived, not brainstormed. (a) STPA. Draw the control structure: owner, coordinator, watcher, children, helpers, checkers, scripts, git, the OS and its power state, the usage meter. Mark the control actions (start, brief, stop, admit a wave, repair, freeze, accept) and the feedback (notes, status files, watcher exits, ledger). For every action, write one row for each of the four unsafe types: not provided; provided when unsafe; too early, too late or out of order; stopped too soon or applied too long. Mark process-model flaws, such as a coordinator believing a stale status file. (b) FMEA. Cross every component with the Avizienis et al. modes plus the language-model modes. (c) Map P1 to P21 onto the rows. A row with no P-id is a candidate missing risk; a P-id with no row shows a gap in the model. (d) Capture-recapture between the STPA list and the FMEA list. (e) Operational feedback (FRACAS: failure reporting, analysis and corrective action): every failure in the ledger is classified to a row.
mechanism.runner: A leaf session, not the coordinator, writes the tables as JSON. A Node script checks that every cell is filled or marked 'not applicable' with a reason, does the mapping, and computes the estimate.
mechanism.when: Before the pilot. Again after the pilot, with the pilot's failure log.
mechanism.input: The protocol, the list of components and actions, the problem list, the pilot ledger.
mechanism.on_failure: If the pilot has a high-severity failure that maps to no row, or the residual estimate is above the owner's threshold, waves do not start until the analysis is redone.

mappings.formula_or_algorithm: Chapman estimator: N = (n1 + 1)(n2 + 1) / (m + 1) - 1, where n1 = items in the STPA list, n2 = items in the FMEA list, m = items in both. Residual = N - (n1 + n2 - m). STPA table rows = control actions x 4. FRACAS escape rate = failures in the ledger that map to no row / all failures in the ledger.
to_measure: n1, n2, m
Number of control actions and feedback paths
Failures in the pilot that map to no row
mappings.effect_on_measures: Quality: fewer surprise failures. Time and tokens: one leaf session plus a script. The estimate turns 'is the list complete?' into a number with stated assumptions.
mappings.build_cost: One leaf session and a script of about 150 lines.

mappings.classical_problem: Watchdog supervision of execution: supervision of being alive, of deadlines, and of logical (program-flow) order. The watchdog must be independent of what it supervises.

solutions.name: Watchdog with a separate time base; time-window watchdog; combined temporal and logical monitoring of program sequence
solutions.source: IEC 61508-7:2010, Annex A (techniques and measures for controlling failures)
solutions.guarantees: A stopped, hung or out-of-sequence execution is detected within a set time.
solutions.assumptions: The watchdog is independent of the supervised process (its own clock and power), and the expected sequence of checkpoints is defined.

solutions.name: Alive, deadline and logical supervision
solutions.source: AUTOSAR Classic Platform, Specification of Watchdog Manager (version not cited)
solutions.guarantees: Separate detectors for 'not running', 'too slow' and 'wrong order or looping'.
solutions.assumptions: Checkpoints are instrumented in the supervised code.

mappings.assumptions_that_fail_here: The watcher runs on the same PC, so sleep and reboot stop both the watcher and the watched: a common mode. Progress for a model is semantic, and a looping session can write new files (padding), so a count of files can be gamed. There is also a contradiction inside the protocol. The progress measure is 'new confirmed cards', but under P1's current rule confirmation happens only after the review, so during Stage A this measure cannot move. The field's answer: define checkpoints that can be checked mechanically; give the watcher a self-check; have someone watch the watcher.

mechanism.rule: Three kinds of supervision for each child. Alive: the transcript file keeps growing. Deadline: each stage checkpoint is reached within its time box. Logical: checkpoints arrive in order: a new question id is covered by a card that passed the script (D4-04), then the pack is frozen, then the review is written. A loop is a repetition of tool-call signatures, or no new question id covered within K cards. The watcher checks itself: on every tick it compares the gap in wall-clock time with the gap in monotonic time (process.hrtime). A gap more than twice the tick means the PC slept, and the watcher exits with the reason 'slept'. It writes its own heartbeat file, and the coordinator checks that file's age on every turn.
mechanism.runner: A Node watcher started by the coordinator in the background for each wave. Its exit wakes the coordinator.
mechanism.input: The child folders, the transcript files (size and the tool-call lines), cards.jsonl, the intake results.
mechanism.on_failure: The exit reason goes to the coordinator. It stops the stalled session first (fail-stop), then restarts the child under D4-07 or drops the field with a note.

mappings.formula_or_algorithm: progress = new distinct question ids covered by cards that passed the script, per unit time. A stall is progress of 0 over T_box. A loop is a Jaccard similarity above J between the last k tool-call signatures (tool name plus hashed arguments). Sleep is detected when (wall-clock delta - monotonic delta) is greater than the tick.
to_measure: Distribution of the time between checkpoints in the pilot
Rate of false stalls
Whether sleep is actually detected: induce a sleep once in the pilot
mappings.effect_on_measures: Time falls because there is no silent waiting. Tokens and cost fall because loops are stopped early.

mappings.classical_problem: Backward error recovery: restarting from a consistent recovery point, with a limit on restarts and escalation of faults that repeat deterministically.

solutions.name: Recovery points and backward error recovery (and the domino effect)
solutions.source: Randell, B. (1975), 'System Structure for Software Fault Tolerance', IEEE Trans. Software Eng. SE-1(2)
solutions.guarantees: Recovery from a consistent saved state. Cascading rollback (the domino effect) is avoided when processes do not exchange messages between their recovery points.
solutions.assumptions: The recovery point is consistent and complete.

solutions.name: Supervision trees with a restart intensity
solutions.source: Armstrong, J. (2003), 'Making reliable distributed systems in the presence of software errors', PhD thesis, KTH
solutions.guarantees: Restart loops are bounded: at most MaxR restarts within MaxT, then escalation to the parent.
solutions.assumptions: Restarts are cheap, and the fault is transient.

solutions.name: Restart cures transient faults (Heisenbugs) but not deterministic ones (Bohrbugs)
solutions.source: Gray, J. (1985), 'Why Do Computers Stop and What Can Be Done About It?', Tandem Technical Report 85.7
solutions.guarantees: Explains why a plain restart recovers most failures in production, and why it cannot recover the rest.
solutions.assumptions: The faults met in production are mostly transient.

mappings.assumptions_that_fail_here: A restart here is expensive. A fault rooted in the brief or the pack recurs on restart: it is a Bohrbug. State that was never written down is lost by definition. An append to cards.jsonl can be torn by a crash. pack.md and cards.jsonl can disagree with each other. The field's answer: atomic writes; validate the checkpoint before restoring; a restart intensity of 1; a fault that recurs is treated as deterministic, so the input is changed, not just the session.

mechanism.rule: (1) Every state file is written to a temporary file and then renamed. On restore, a JSONL file is validated line by line and a torn last line is dropped. (2) The restore is validated before any replacement starts. The pack hash must equal the frozen record, and the cards must be schema-valid and agree with the pack. (3) At most 1 restart per field per stage. A second failure at the same stage escalates to the owner, or the field is dropped with a note. (4) The reason for each restart is recorded. If the same failure class recurs, the brief or pack is repaired before any further session starts.
mechanism.runner: The coordinator runs restore-check.js before it starts the replacement. The restart counter is kept in the coordinator's status file.
mechanism.when: On every restart, and when a coordinator hands over.
mechanism.input: The field folder, the frozen pack hash, cards.jsonl, the status file. The status file carries a sequence number, and the coordinator refuses one older than the last it saw.
mechanism.on_failure: If the pack is invalid, restore from cards.jsonl. If the cards are invalid too, the field is dropped and the owner is told.

mappings.formula_or_algorithm: MaxR = 1 per stage. Spend wasted on restarts is at most (MaxR + 1) x the cost of a stage.
to_measure: Restarts per field, with their cause and outcome
Torn lines found on restore
Repeated failures of the same class
mappings.effect_on_measures: Cost and tokens are bounded: no restart storms. Quality: no restart from a corrupt or stale state.
mappings.build_cost: A script of about 120 lines, plus a write helper shared by all the scripts.

mappings.classical_problem: Recovery block: a primary, an acceptance test, and an alternate that runs from saved state. The alternate path is exercised only rarely.

solutions.name: Recovery blocks
solutions.source: Randell, B. (1975), 'System Structure for Software Fault Tolerance', IEEE Trans. Software Eng. SE-1(2)
solutions.guarantees: A failure of the primary is masked, provided the acceptance test detects it and the alternate runs from a restored, consistent state.
solutions.assumptions: The acceptance test is effective and independent. The alternate works.

solutions.name: End-to-end argument (state that was never recorded cannot be checked)
solutions.source: Saltzer, J.H., Reed, D.P., Clark, D.D. (1984), 'End-to-End Arguments in System Design', ACM Trans. Computer Systems 2(4)
solutions.guarantees: Only what reaches the endpoint in a form that can be checked can be verified.
solutions.assumptions: As in D4-03.

mappings.assumptions_that_fail_here: Under amendment 1, the fresh-session review is the alternate path, taken after a crash or a full window. It is an exception, so it is rarely exercised and therefore untested at the moment it is needed. What the researcher read but did not write down can enter the review only as uncited judgment sentences, and no check covers those. My field cannot say which of the two writes better reviews; no source compares them for this job. It does say two things. The alternate must be exercised. The configuration in which every input to a checked output is recorded can be checked; the other cannot be.

mechanism.rule: The pilot writes both reviews, as amendment 3 recommends. They are adjudicated blind by the same acceptance test: the end-to-end check of D4-03, the judgment check of conditions, and the planted defects of D4-11. Whichever form is chosen, the fresh-from-pack path runs at least once per wave, so that the alternate stays tested.
mechanism.runner: The coordinator starts both reviews in the pilot. Scripts score them.
mechanism.input: The frozen pack, the must-read sections, our files with plants, both reviews.
mechanism.on_failure: The owner chooses from the scores. If the alternate fails in a wave where it was exercised, the restart path of D4-07 is marked unsafe until it is repaired.

mappings.formula_or_algorithm: For each review: e2e failure rate; rate of use outside conditions; plants found out of k; share of sentences labelled judgment (an output of the same-session review that cannot be checked); tokens.
to_measure: Share of judgment sentences in each form
Failure rate of cited sentences in each form
Plants detected in each form
Tokens per review in each form
mappings.effect_on_measures: Quality and hallucinations are measured, not assumed. Tokens: one extra review in the pilot, and one exercise of the alternate per wave.

mappings.classical_problem: Acceptance sampling by attributes, with rectifying inspection. A sample whose result cannot reject the lot gives no protection.

solutions.name: Rectifying sampling inspection (a rejected lot is 100 % inspected; LTPD and AOQL plans)
solutions.source: Dodge, H.F. & Romig, H.G. (1929), 'A Method of Sampling Inspection', Bell System Technical Journal 8
solutions.guarantees: A known operating characteristic curve, P(accept | defect rate p), and a bound on the defect rate that passes through.
solutions.assumptions: Random sampling, a homogeneous lot, perfect inspection.

solutions.name: Sampling by attributes indexed by acceptance quality limit
solutions.source: ISO 2859-1, 'Sampling procedures for inspection by attributes'
solutions.guarantees: Standard tables of sample size and acceptance number.
solutions.assumptions: A continuing series of lots.

mappings.assumptions_that_fail_here: Inspection is not perfect, so use the detection rate d measured in D4-01. Lots are not homogeneous: cards differ by reader and by type of source, so sample each reader separately. Sampling must be random by script, not left to the checker's choice. The 100 % check of cited cards is already the strongest plan for that critical subset. The open question is the cards no one cites. They still shape judgment, and they count toward coverage under P13.

mechanism.rule: For each field and each reader's cards, draw a zero-acceptance sample (c = 0) of n cards that no conclusion cites. One semantic failure (wrong number or wrong conditions) means that reader's cards are all checked, or removed from the pack and listed as not covered. Amendment 3 turned the 95 % gate into a ledger measure with no action, and that removed the plan's protection.
mechanism.runner: sample.js picks the cards with a recorded random seed. The fixed-brief checker checks them. The coordinator applies the result at gate A.
mechanism.when: At gate A, before the pack is frozen and before the review (phase containment).
mechanism.input: cards.jsonl, grouped by reader; d from D4-01.
mechanism.on_failure: Rectify the reader's cards (check them all) or quarantine them.

mappings.formula_or_algorithm: Pa(p) = (1 - d*p)^n. Sample size for a lot tolerance p1 at consumer risk beta: n = ln(beta) / ln(1 - d*p1). Example: p1 = 0.10, beta = 0.10, d = 1 gives n = 22; d = 0.8 gives n = 28.
to_measure: Lot size per reader
Failures in the sample
d from D4-01
The random seed used
mappings.effect_on_measures: Hallucinations in the knowledge no one cites fall. Tokens: n checks per reader, far fewer than checking everything.
mappings.build_cost: A script of about 60 lines and one rule at gate A.

mappings.classical_problem: Use outside the assumed conditions: a correct component reused where its assumptions do not hold.

solutions.name: Lesson from Ariane 501: reused software whose assumptions were not checked against the new conditions
solutions.source: Lions, J.-L. et al. (1996), 'ARIANE 5 Flight 501 Failure: Report by the Inquiry Board'
solutions.guarantees: The rule that assumptions must be stated and checked against each new context of use.
solutions.assumptions: Not applicable.

solutions.name: Explicit context and assumption nodes in an assurance argument
solutions.source: Kelly, T.P. (1998), 'Arguing Safety: A Systematic Approach to Managing Safety Cases', PhD thesis, University of York
solutions.guarantees: Every claim carries the context it holds in, so a mismatch can be seen.
solutions.assumptions: Contexts are stated in a vocabulary shared with the place they are used.

mappings.assumptions_that_fail_here: Conditions are written in prose. Reviews paraphrase. Ranges ('repositories of 10k to 100k lines') rarely match the vocabulary of a claim. The field's answer is to make the precondition mechanical wherever the vocabulary allows, and to leave the model's judgment only for what remains.

mechanism.rule: Card conditions are typed fields with a controlled vocabulary: task type, model family, repository size range, language, metric. Each citing sentence carries an applies_to record in the same fields. A script flags any applies_to value outside the card's range, and any condition the card has that the sentence leaves out (a dropped condition). Only flagged sentences, and conditions in free text, go to the model's judgment check.
mechanism.runner: context-check.js, run by the coordinator after each review and after the synthesis.
mechanism.when: After each review and after the synthesis.
mechanism.input: The review and synthesis claim records; cards.jsonl.
mechanism.on_failure: The sentence is marked 'outside conditions' and either relabelled as judgment or removed. The rate is recorded in the ledger.

mappings.formula_or_algorithm: Pass when, for every field f: applies_to[f] is within card.conditions[f], and every f that is set on the card is also set on the sentence.
to_measure: Share of conditions that fit the typed fields
Rate of flags
How often the checker agrees with the script's flags
mappings.effect_on_measures: Hallucinations (misapplied claims) fall. Tokens fall, because the model checks only flagged sentences.
mappings.build_cost: A field schema plus a script of about 100 lines.

mappings.classical_problem: Qualifying a verifier by known-answer tests, with an oracle independent of the party being tested. Defects seeded into the material under review measure the reviewer.

solutions.name: Independent verification and validation (technical, managerial and financial independence)
solutions.source: IEEE Std 1012, 'Standard for System, Software, and Hardware Verification and Validation'
solutions.guarantees: Whoever sets the oracle is not the party being judged.
solutions.assumptions: An independent party with the knowledge to judge exists.

solutions.name: Error seeding applied to a reviewer
solutions.source: Mills, H.D. (1972), 'On the Statistical Validation of Computer Programs', IBM FSD report FSC-72-6015
solutions.guarantees: A measured rate at which the reviewer finds defects.
solutions.assumptions: Plants are representative, and the reviewer does not know about them.

solutions.name: Perspective-based reading (inspectors with assigned perspectives, with measured detection)
solutions.source: Basili, V.R., Green, S., Laitenberger, O., Lanubile, F., Shull, F., Sorumgard, S., Zelkowitz, M.V. (1996), 'The Empirical Investigation of Perspective-Based Reading', Empirical Software Engineering 1(2)
solutions.guarantees: Inspectors given different perspectives find different defects.
solutions.assumptions: Human inspectors.

mappings.assumptions_that_fail_here: Technical independence is impossible within one model. A model may spot a plant as a plant. With 2 to 4 plants per expert, no rate can be estimated for one expert; the plants only catch gross failure. The rate can be pooled across experts for the programme as a whole. The current certification checks the expert's inputs (coverage, reading list, confirmed citations). It certifies the evidence, not the reviewer's ability to find what is wrong in our work.

mechanism.rule: Plant k = 2 to 4 known defects in the copies of our work that each expert is given. Each plant rests on a confirmed card. Examples: a design that assumes a result holds for a model or repository size that the card excludes; a quoted number that has been altered. At least one plant contradicts the answer we hope for, which tests for anchoring (P2). The expert is not told. Certification also requires that at least the owner's threshold of plants be found. The plants are then stripped from the review output using the key.
mechanism.runner: The coordinator runs plant.js before the review and score-plants.js after it. The key is held outside every child's folder.
mechanism.input: Our work files as copies; confirmed cards.
mechanism.on_failure: An expert that misses every plant has its review labelled uncertified. One re-review is allowed from a fresh session (restart intensity 1, D4-07).

mappings.formula_or_algorithm: With k plants and detection d, P(all found) = d^k. Pool across experts to estimate d for the programme: total found / total planted, with a Clopper-Pearson interval. Track the plant that runs against our hopes separately, as an anchoring rate.
to_measure: Plants found per expert
Plants against our hopes found, compared with neutral plants found
Plants falsely reported
Change in the review's tokens
mappings.effect_on_measures: Quality: experts are certified on what they do, not only on their inputs. Anchoring becomes a measured quantity. Tokens: slight.
mappings.build_cost: Two scripts (about 150 lines), plus the coordinator writing the plants from confirmed cards.

mappings.classical_problem: Closing a hazard log: a hazard, here a dismissal, may be closed only with verification evidence and acceptance by an independent party. Closures can be reopened.

solutions.name: Hazard tracking to closure, with verification evidence
solutions.source: MIL-STD-882E (2012), 'Department of Defense Standard Practice: System Safety'
solutions.guarantees: No hazard is silently dropped. Each closure is traceable to evidence and to the party that accepted it.
solutions.assumptions: Whoever accepts a closure is independent and competent.

mappings.assumptions_that_fail_here: The refuter is the same model as the reviewer that dismissed the lead (common mode, D4-02). Nobody knows the refuter's rate of misses. The field's answer is to require evidence for a closure and to measure the refuter by seeding.

mechanism.rule: Every dismissal ('wrong form', 'wrong problem', a dropped field) is an entry in a log, with a reason class and the confirmed cards that show it. A dismissal without a confirmed card stays open, labelled 'judgment'. A new card that contradicts a dismissal reopens it. The refuter's input includes 2 or 3 seeded false dismissals of leads that confirmed cards support.
mechanism.runner: A script builds the log from the review files. The refuter session attacks every entry. The coordinator closes only entries that have evidence.
mechanism.when: After the reviews, before the synthesis.
mechanism.input: Review files, confirmed cards, seeded false dismissals.
mechanism.on_failure: If the refuter misses the seeded dismissals, its 'upheld' verdicts are labelled unqualified, and those dismissals go to the owner as open entries.

mappings.formula_or_algorithm: Refuter detection = seeded dismissals caught / seeded dismissals. Share of the log closed with evidence.
to_measure: Seeded dismissals caught
Share of dismissals with a confirmed card behind them
Dismissals reopened
mappings.effect_on_measures: Quality: fewer wrongly dismissed leads. Tokens: small.
mappings.build_cost: A log script of about 80 lines plus seeds.

missing_risks.title: Detectors with no measured coverage: a count of zero failures read as quality
missing_risks.classical_name: Latent faults in safety mechanisms; diagnostic coverage; proof testing (IEC 61508)
missing_risks.why_it_applies: The ledger counts the failures each checker found. A checker that does not work reports few failures and looks like a high-quality field. Nothing in the list measures a detector.
missing_risks.mechanism: D4-01: blind seeding per fault class, with a proof-test seed in every wave.

missing_risks.title: A check that could not run is counted as a pass
missing_risks.classical_name: Fail-safe defaults; fail-open safety mechanism (Saltzer, J.H. & Schroeder, M.D. (1975), 'The Protection of Information in Computer Systems', Proc. IEEE 63(9))
missing_risks.why_it_applies: Pages that are blocked, PDFs, timeouts, a crash in the schema or quote script, a checker that cannot open a source: unless results have three values, any of these can slip through as 'no failure found'.
missing_risks.mechanism: Every check returns pass, fail or not-run. Not-run is shown and counted, and is never treated as a pass. Gates count not-run against their threshold.

missing_risks.title: The layers of defence fail together
missing_risks.classical_name: Common-cause failure across layers of defence in depth (the 'Swiss cheese' model: Reason, J. (1990), 'Human Error', Cambridge University Press)
missing_risks.why_it_applies: Readers, checkers, refuter, reviewer and mapper are all one model family. Multiplying the miss rates of the layers as if they were independent overstates the protection. P20 names this only for checker against checked, not across the whole stack.
missing_risks.mechanism: Measure the joint miss rate on seeded items across the layers in sequence (D4-02 formula, applied to layers). Report the measured end-to-end escape rate, not a product of rates.

missing_risks.title: Single-version scripts as single points of failure
missing_risks.classical_name: The voter or adjudicator as a single point of failure in N-version systems
missing_risks.why_it_applies: The schema checker, the synthesis, the end-to-end check, the watcher and the token counter are each one piece of untested code. A bug in any of them passes or drops everything, in every field.
missing_risks.mechanism: Mutation-test each script before the pilot. Known-bad inputs (the seeded set of D4-01) must be rejected and known-good ones accepted. The test runs whenever a script changes.

missing_risks.title: Gates become measures and drift is accepted
missing_risks.classical_name: Normalization of deviance (Vaughan, D. (1996), 'The Challenger Launch Decision', University of Chicago Press)
missing_risks.why_it_applies: Amendment 3 already turned the 95 % gate into a ledger measure with no action attached. Rates that have no action line creep up, and each wave accepts the level the last one reached.
missing_risks.mechanism: Before the pilot, every ledger measure gets an action line set by the owner, and a script compares the measure with the line at each wave gate.

missing_risks.title: Recovery and hand-over paths that never run
missing_risks.classical_name: Untested alternates and failover paths (recovery-block alternates; latent faults in redundant paths)
missing_risks.why_it_applies: The fresh-session restart, the coordinator's hand-over at 200,000 tokens, the watcher's detection of sleep, and the escalation for a missing allowance are taken only when something has already failed. Their first use would be in an emergency.
missing_risks.mechanism: Fault injection into the harness during the pilot: kill one child, put the PC to sleep once, force one coordinator hand-over, and record whether each path recovers.

missing_risks.title: Recovery from a stale or inconsistent state
missing_risks.classical_name: Inconsistent recovery point; a flaw in the controller's process model (STPA)
missing_risks.why_it_applies: The coordinator decides from status files. A status file written before a crash, or a pack whose hash disagrees with cards.jsonl, gives a wrong picture of where a field stands, and the coordinator acts on it.
missing_risks.mechanism: Status files carry a sequence number and a timestamp, and an older file is refused. Restore validation as in D4-07.

do_not: Do not take agreement between instances of one model as independent confirmation, and do not multiply their error rates as if they were independent (Knight & Leveson 1986).
Do not report a count of failed citations without the checker's measured detection rate: zero found is not zero present.
Do not let a check that could not run count as a pass.
Do not rely on checks at each hop in place of one end-to-end check against the source bytes. Checks at each hop only reduce how often the end-to-end check fails.
Do not turn a gate into a ledger measure unless an action threshold is fixed in advance.
Do not vote with two versions. Two can detect a fault, not decide it. Settle a disagreement with an acceptance test tied to the source.

Do not add redundancy (second experts, extra checkers, extra refuters) before its independence has been measured. Same-model redundancy adds cost and complexity and little coverage against design faults (Leveson 2011).
Do not let a checker learn which items are seeded or planted, or take its brief from the party it checks.
Do not keep a recovery path that never runs.
Do not restart a failed session again and again from the same inputs. After one restart, change the input or escalate.
Do not claim the problem list is complete. State the method, the model it rests on, and the estimated residual.
Do not check cards only after the review: an unchecked card in the expert's window shapes uncited judgment that no later check sees.
not_my_field: P5: text in a web page steering a session is prompt injection, which belongs to security and to capability confinement. My field adds only that a reader's output passes through a schema acting as a fault-containment boundary.
P6 and P7: concurrent writers, single-writer ownership and a shared register that races belong to distributed systems and concurrency control.

P8, P11, P12 and P14: fan-out, admission control, the coordinator's window and cost estimation belong to scheduling, capacity planning and operations research. My field adds only that each stop threshold must be fixed in advance and have a runner.
P16: selection bias in search belongs to systematic-review methodology (the evidence-synthesis field).
P18: whether the tree beats one session is a question of experimental design. Hatton, L. (1997), 'N-version design versus one good version', IEEE Software 14(6), is an analogy only.
P2: anchoring as a cognitive bias belongs to human factors and psychology. My field contributes only the blind plant that runs against our hopes (D4-11).

S: the tree's shape, its branching and the B+ tree analogy belong to data structures and distributed systems. My field adds only fault-containment regions (no messages between children, which avoids the domino effect) and the restart intensity of D4-07.
